cards.title: Strictness of the polynomial hierarchy
cards.formal: For every integer \(k\ge0\), is \(\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\subsetneq\Sigma_{k+1}^{\mathrm P}\)? In other words, must each additional fixed block of polynomially bounded alternating Boolean quantifiers enable a decision language that cannot be expressed with k blocks? The classes are the uniform, unrelativized classes defined below.
cards.definitions: All languages are subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\); membership is a total yes/no decision on every finite binary string. Let \(\Sigma_0^{\mathrm P}=\Pi_0^{\mathrm P}=\mathrm P\), where P consists of languages decided by a single deterministic multitape Turing machine within \(C(n+1)^d\) transitions on every length-n string, for fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\). Machines have a finite program, fixed finite alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. For fixed \(k\ge1\), a language L belongs to \(\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\) if there exist integers \(a\ge1,b\ge0\) and one deterministic polynomial-time Boolean predicate R such that for every x, with \(n=|x|\) and \(p(n)=a(n+1)^b\), \(x\in L\iff\exists y_1\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\ \forall y_2\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\cdots Q_k y_k\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\ R(x,y_1,\ldots,y_k)=1\). Here \(Q_i\) is existential for odd i and universal for even i. An entire string is chosen in each block; k does not count individual quantified bits. To fix the predicate input, encode a tuple by concatenating \(1^{|s|}0s\) for each of its k+1 components in order. R is computed by one machine in the model above, halting within \(C(M+1)^d\) on all length-M strings for fixed C,d and rejecting malformed tuple encodings. Runtime counts all transitions and all input bits. Restricting the common witness bound to this form of p loses no languages, because a larger polynomial bound can pad each witness and ignore unused bits. The integers, machines and time bounds may depend on L and on the fixed k, but not on x or the quantified strings. Define \(\Pi_k^{\mathrm P}=\{\{0,1\}^*\setminus L:L\in\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\}\) and \(\mathrm{PH}=\bigcup_{k\ge0}\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\). Thus \(\Sigma_1^{\mathrm P}=\mathrm{NP}\) and \(\Pi_1^{\mathrm P}=\mathrm{coNP}\). No advice, random bits, quantum operations, external oracle or promise inputs are present. The inclusion between consecutive existential levels always holds; strictness means that there exists a language \(L_k\in\Sigma_{k+1}^{\mathrm P}\setminus\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\). This language may depend on k; there is no added requirement of an effective generator for all separating languages.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of strict containment for every nonnegative integer k, or prove that \(\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}=\Sigma_{k+1}^{\mathrm P}\) for some fixed nonnegative integer k. The negative answer is exactly the logical negation, since the inclusions are unconditional. Equality at one adjacent pair collapses all higher finite levels. A separation of finitely many initial levels, an oracle separation, or a collapse conditional on an unproved hypothesis is insufficient to settle the displayed all-level assertion. No concrete finite input is required as a witness to a class equality or separation.
cards.why: This is the organizing conjecture behind the computational cost of alternating existential and universal reasoning. It strengthens the basic P-versus-NP distinction across all fixed quantifier depths and underlies many conditional lower bounds in complexity, verification, and graph problems with nested solution requirements.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture asserting that every further alternation increases computational power. It governs a large family of complexity classifications and has major circuit-lower-bound consequences.

progress.text: Meyer and Stockmeyer introduce the hierarchy, and Stockmeyer develops its structure and complete problems. The source survey traces this history and gives the quantified-predicate definition used here.

Karp–Lipton relates polynomial-size circuits for NP to a collapse of PH; Yao and Håstad establish infinitude in a suitably chosen oracle world. These concern a conditional implication and a relativized separation, respectively.
Rossman, Servedio and Tan prove that a random oracle gives an infinite polynomial hierarchy with probability one. Each binary string independently belongs to that oracle with probability one half.
Wigderson’s book still states strictness of successive unrelativized levels as a conjecture and distinguishes fixed-depth quantification from unrestricted polynomial-space reasoning.

Hirsch and Volkovich’s revised paper compares classes associated with the Linear Ordering Principle and strengthens Karp–Lipton-style conditional conclusions. Its assumptions do not establish an unconditional collapse of PH.

The checked 2026 revision supplies conditional collapses and related containments, while the 2015 theorem is relativized. context_blocks.text: NP captures a single existential choice of a certificate. A second block permits a statement of the form “there is a candidate that survives every challenge”; a third permits a response to every challenge. Polynomially many bits may be chosen at each stage. The question is whether every additional fixed stage enables some decision problem that cannot be expressed with fewer stages and a polynomial-time final check.

The hierarchy is monotone because an additional unused block is harmless. Equality of neighboring levels would make all subsequent levels equal as well, a standard collapse property of bounded alternation. Thus the negative answer asserts a finite level at which the hierarchy stabilizes; it does not require separating or collapsing every level independently.

Strictness includes \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) at its first step, but \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone would leave the possibility of a later collapse. The conjecture also implies that PH is a proper subclass of PSPACE: if TQBF belonged to PH, it would belong to one fixed level, and PSPACE-completeness would force the whole hierarchy into that level. Allowing arbitrarily many quantifier alternations in the input is therefore a separate issue from allowing any fixed number.

The Karp–Lipton implication connects this conjecture to circuit complexity. Polynomial-size circuits for NP would collapse PH, so an infinite hierarchy would imply an NP language without polynomial-size circuits. Conditional collapse arguments are useful precisely because they can turn an assumption about nonuniform circuits into a conclusion about uniform classes; the conditional conclusion is not an established collapse.

Rossman, Servedio, and Tan prove that PH is infinite relative to a random oracle with probability one, through an average-case circuit-depth hierarchy theorem. Random membership bits supplied by an oracle are an extra computational resource. The result shows that strictness is compatible with, and typical in, that oracle model; it leaves the unrelativized hierarchy open.

The quantifier count is fixed separately for each class. It does not describe an algorithm that receives an arbitrary level number and solves all those levels with one common polynomial bound. Similarly, strictness may use a different separating language at every level, and the statement does not impose a uniform procedure generating all such languages.

cards.title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
cards.formal: Is classical Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every pair of integers \(C\ge1,c\ge1\), does there exist a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Extended Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\) has binary encoding length \(|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+2)^c\)? The formula and proof encodings and the fixed proof rules are specified below.
cards.definitions:
A propositional formula is a finite syntax tree built from variables \(v_i\), indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\), unary negation and binary material implication. Its Boolean value under an assignment \(v_i\mapsto\{0,1\}\) is defined recursively, with \(A	o B\) false exactly when A is true and B is false. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. Let code(a), for \(a\ge0\), be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, with \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)floor+1\). Encode \(v_i\) as 00 followed by code(i), \(
eg A\) as 01 followed by the encoding of A, and \(A	o B\) as 10 followed by the encodings of A and B. This prefix syntax contains the whole formula tree, not a circuit or a program generating it; \(|\varphi|\) is its bit length. Fix the three classical Frege axiom schemes \(A	o(B	o A)\), \((A	o(B	o C))	o((A	o B)	o(A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o
eg A)	o(A	o B)\). An instance substitutes arbitrary formulas for A, B and C consistently. Modus ponens infers B from two earlier lines A and \(A	o B\). An extension introduction adds two consecutive lines \(e	o	heta\) and \(	heta	o e\), where e is a variable absent from the target formula, theta and every line before this pair. The defining formula theta may use variables of the target and previously introduced extension variables, so definitions are acyclic. Freshness is checked before the pair, not between its two lines. There are no unproved hypotheses. A proof is a finite nonempty list of lines justified by these axiom schemes, modus ponens or such an extension pair; its last line is exactly the target formula and contains no extension variables. Earlier lines can be cited any number of times. There is no depth bound, tree-like proof restriction or restriction on the sizes of intermediate formulas. For a complete proof encoding, first write code(m) for its number of lines, and then encode each line with a two-bit tag, its metadata and its entire formula in the prefix syntax above. Tag 00 stores the axiom-scheme number 1, 2 or 3 with code; tag 01 stores with code the two earlier, one-based line indices for modus ponens, in the order A then A implies B; tag 10 stores with code the index of the fresh extension variable and must be followed immediately by a tag-11 line giving the reverse implication for the same definition. Tag 11 has no metadata and is valid only as that second line of an extension pair. The first extension formula uniquely determines theta, and both implication formulas are fully written and counted. Missing or trailing bits and invalid justifications are rejected. The proof length counts all bits, including the line count, formulas, variable indices, rule tags and inference references. This is a fixed polynomial-time checkable presentation of classical EF, polynomially equivalent to the usual finite Frege bases with extension. EF is complete, so every tautology has some finite proof; the issue is a common polynomial bound. The chosen binary encoding and paired extension rule fix presentation details without changing polynomial boundedness. The hard formula may depend on C and c; no polynomial-time procedure generating a hard family is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed lower-bound assertion or its logical negation. The affirmative answer must, for every polynomial bound \(C(n+2)^c\), establish a tautology whose every valid EF proof exceeds that bound. The negative answer must establish fixed integers C,c for which every tautology has some valid EF proof of length at most \(C(|\varphi|+2)^c\); it need not give a polynomial-time proof-search algorithm. A bound for one search procedure, for bounded-depth or ordinary Frege, for a different logic, or for an algebraic encoding without a valid polynomial-size propositional translation does not settle this target.
cards.why: Extended Frege captures a powerful form of efficient propositional reasoning with reusable definitions. A superpolynomial lower bound would cross one of the central barriers in proof complexity and clarify whether a standard, highly expressive certificate language necessarily fails on some short true statements.

importance.reason: A defining open lower-bound problem for strong propositional reasoning, closely connected to bounded arithmetic, circuit complexity, and the limits of efficiently checkable certificates.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow define propositional proof-system efficiency and formalize the extension rule. Their equivalence theorems make EF polynomial boundedness independent of standard presentations; Cook’s posted correction to Corollary 4.7 keeps the coNP-versus-NP premise explicit.

Wigderson’s book lists superpolynomial unrestricted Frege lower bounds as open and distinguishes the additional sharing available in Extended Frege. Lower bounds for the weaker system would not automatically apply to EF.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) with additional formal provability hypotheses. The checked preprint does not give an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh, Jain, Li and Mathialagan construct succinct non-interactive arguments for NP under promise derandomization, LWE, SXDH and a bounded-arithmetic hardness-certification assumption. The formal unprovability premise differs from the unconditional proof-size target.

Alekseev’s journal paper proves an exponential bit-size lower bound for algebraic Binary Value Principle refutations and explicitly explains why it does not give a Frege or EF lower bound for propositional tautologies.

Akbar Tabatabai reports exponential separations between EF systems for intuitionistic substructural and linear logics. The preprint’s stated scope differs from this classical system; its proof was not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: Extension variables let a proof name a formula once and reuse its name. This can represent shared computations economically, as a Boolean circuit shares intermediate gates. Expanding all abbreviations into formula trees can cause an exponential increase in length, so a lower bound that counts only ordinary Frege proofs does not automatically survive the extension rule.

The question concerns the existence of short certificates, not the time required to discover them. A particular proof search method might take exponential time even though another method could find a short proof; conversely, a proof-size lower bound would constrain every method that outputs an EF derivation. The input length is the final tautology’s actual encoding length, so a lower bound exponential in a smaller hidden parameter may still be only polynomial in the input.

If \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\), every polynomial-time verifiable propositional proof system has hard tautologies, including EF. The converse for this particular system is unknown: showing that EF is inefficient does not rule out a different proof system that gives short certificates for all tautologies. This is why an EF lower bound would be a major advance without automatically constituting a proof of \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\). Cook’s author page corrects the premise of Corollary 4.7 in the original paper to coNP differing from NP; a P-versus-NP separation alone is not the stated premise.

Recent algebraic lower bounds illustrate an encoding issue. Alekseev proves exponential bit-size lower bounds for an extension of polynomial calculus that can simulate EF on suitable propositional translations. The hard Binary Value Principle instance is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size CNF. The paper explicitly explains that its result therefore does not yield a Frege or EF lower bound.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) under additional bounded-arithmetic assumptions. This explores the consequences of proof-complexity hypotheses without proving an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh and coauthors construct succinct arguments under derandomization, cryptographic, and formal unprovability assumptions. Their result connects the difficulty of certifying hard tautologies to cryptography; it does not establish the unconditional size lower bound asked for here.

The use of classical implication matters. Recent lower bounds for Extended Frege systems of intuitionistic or linear logics concern different rules and valid formulas. The August 2026 preprint on those systems therefore cannot be read as a solution of the unrestricted classical problem fixed here.

cards.title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: For every real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge3\) such that no q-SAT decider A has a bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F, for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The width q may depend on epsilon but is fixed independently of the input. Equivalently, is \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\)? This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. The sequence \(s_q\) is nondecreasing: a decider for width q+1 also decides the width-q restriction after checking its syntax. Since every \(s_q\le1\), its limit exists. The quantified statement says that no fixed positive saving from the exponent 1 works for all fixed widths. Its negation is that there exists one real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that for each integer \(q\ge3\) there are a q-SAT decider \(A_q\) and constants \(C_q,d_q\) with \(t_{A_q}(F)\le C_q2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_q}\) for every q-CNF formula F. The algorithm and polynomial factor may depend on q and the selected epsilon. There is no added requirement of one algorithm receiving q as an input, nor of an effective procedure generating \(A_q\) from q. Each individual machine is uniform over its formula inputs. Infima need not be attained; the equivalence uses the available slack between a limit below 1 and 1.

cards.title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic algorithm A, a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge0\), such that A decides whether G contains a k-clique and uses at most \(f(k)(N+2)^c\) steps for every encoded pair (G,k) of total bit length N? The exponent c is independent of both k and G. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\) under parameterized many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: A graph G is finite, simple and undirected, with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), including n=0. A k-clique is a subset of exactly k vertices with an edge between each pair of distinct vertices. The empty subset is a 0-clique; no k-clique exists when k>n. For a fixed binary encoding, write \(1^n0\), then the n by n adjacency matrix in row order, then the ordinary binary representation of the nonnegative integer k (0 is written as 0, and otherwise there are no leading zeroes). A valid matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, and the entire remaining suffix is the representation of k. N counts all bits, including k. A rejects any malformed string in time polynomial in its bit length. The bound in the statement applies to every valid pair, including k>n. The parameter is k alone; there is no promise on density, degree, clique number or any other graph property. A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes only at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The runtime includes parsing, input access and all internal work. Correctness is exact, and no advice, randomness, oracle or quantum operations are supplied. The same A, f and c work for every pair; f must be computable by a machine that halts on every nonnegative integer input, but its growth and the time needed to compute it have no prescribed bound. Constant multiplicative overhead can be absorbed into f. Using full input length rather than n gives the usual FPT question: for k at most n the two lengths are polynomially related, and k>n is rejected after parsing. For completeness, a parameterized language is a set of pairs \((x,k)\in\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\), with both components explicitly encoded. It belongs to FPT if one uniform deterministic machine decides it within \(h(k)(M+2)^a\) steps for a total computable positive h, a fixed nonnegative integer a and complete encoding length M. A parameterized many-one reduction computes a single output pair \((y,k^{\prime})\) in such a time bound, preserves yes versus no membership, and satisfies \(k^{\prime}\le g(k)\) for a total computable function g; writing the output counts toward its runtime. The class W[1] can equivalently be defined as all parameterized languages admitting such a reduction to the Clique problem just specified. This characterization fixes the reduction convention without a change of target. It includes FPT, and Clique belongs to it, so FPT membership of Clique is equivalent to equality of the two classes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the single algorithm, computable multiplier and constant exponent in the statement, or prove their joint nonexistence. In the affirmative case, prove correctness and the uniform worst-case bound on all pairs, together with the malformed-input convention. In the negative case, exclude every such algorithm, computable f and exponent c; a conditional lower bound, a bound for a restricted algorithm model, or failure at one proposed multiplier and exponent does not settle this target. An algorithm whose polynomial exponent depends on k also does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.
cards.why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) meets the requested form, while \(n^{k/10}\) does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\) is a stronger separation conjecture than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) problem in FPT time. This is why a \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\).

Uniformity is essential: one finite program must handle every k. Neither a separately chosen algorithm for each fixed k nor a bound with an exponent that increases with k establishes FPT. Conversely, the allowed computable multiplier can be enormous; this is a structural tractability question and does not assert that an affirmative algorithm would be practical.

cards.title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is \(s_3>0\) in the deterministic bit model defined below? Equivalently, does there exist one real \(c>0\) such that no 3-SAT decider A has a runtime bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{c n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) on every valid 3-CNF formula F for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The same positive c must exclude all such algorithms. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. This card specializes q to 3. Its negation, \(s_3=0\), means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a 3-SAT decider \(A_\varepsilon\) with fixed constants \(C_\varepsilon,d_\varepsilon\) satisfying \(t_{A_\varepsilon}(F)\le C_\varepsilon 2^{\varepsilon n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_\varepsilon}\) on every valid formula. The machine and constants may depend on epsilon. This statement does not require one machine with a single subexponential runtime bound, nor a computable map from epsilon to a machine.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(s_3>0\) or of \(s_3=0\) for the explicitly defined rate. A positive answer requires a positive constant excluding every valid deterministic decider at that exponential rate, with any polynomial input factor. A negative answer must establish arbitrarily small attainable positive exponents with the stated quantifiers. A fixed improved positive exponent, a bound for a restricted algorithm class, or a conditional lower bound does not settle this question. No numerical estimate of \(s_3\) is requested: the target is its strict positivity.
cards.why: ETH is the central hypothesis for ruling out subexponential exact algorithms and many fixed-parameter speedups. It turns the qualitative P versus NP question into a quantitative claim that can be transferred through carefully sized reductions.

importance.reason: A foundational quantitative hardness hypothesis underlying exact, parameterized, graph, and geometric algorithm lower bounds.

context_blocks.text: NP-completeness describes the possibility of polynomial-time algorithms and does not itself impose a positive exponential rate. Even if P differs from NP, a running time such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\) remains possible for 3-SAT. ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size \(n^{3}\), which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one \(2^{o(n)}\) algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

Liu’s deterministic algorithm has runtime \(O(1.32793^n)\) up to polynomial input factors. It therefore supplies an upper bound on \(s_3\); it establishes neither a positive lower bound nor the value of \(s_3\). The existence of one algorithm with a positive exponential rate does not rule out a much faster algorithm. Empirical solver success and promises on the formula are also distinct from this all-input infimum.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.

A single fixed exponent in ETH must obstruct every algorithm. Refuting one proposed lower-bound constant does not suffice, because another smaller positive constant could still work. Conversely, a refutation may use a different finite algorithm for each desired exponent; no effective procedure generating those algorithms is added to the target.

cards.title: Integer factorization in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,c\ge0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm A such that, for every positive integer N in binary, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N with probability at least \(2/3\), and for every random-bit sequence halts within \(C(n+1)^c\) bit steps, where \(n=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor+1\)? The same A, C and c must work for all N.
cards.definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two representation of N, with no leading zeroes; its length n counts bits, not the numerical value of N. The one-character string 1 represents N=1. The empty string and all strings beginning with 0 are invalid and must be rejected on every random-bit sequence within the same polynomial bound in their length. For \(N\ge2\), the unique correct factorization is the finite list \((p_1,e_1),\ldots,(p_r,e_r)\), where \(p_1<\cdots<p_r\) are primes, each \(e_i\) is a positive integer, and \(N=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}\). A prime is an integer at least 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. The correct list for N=1 is empty. To fix a binary output format, encode a nonnegative integer a by \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary representation of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). A successful output is 1 followed by code(r) and then code(p_i), code(e_i) for i in increasing order, with no other bits; the single bit 0 is the failure or invalid-input symbol. A is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with one finite program, a fixed finite number of tapes and fixed finite alphabets. It has a read-only input tape and initially blank work and output tapes; a transition accesses only cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. It may request one new independent fair bit at a transition. The probability space is \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) with independent uniform coordinates, and the probability guarantee is separate for every fixed input N. The runtime is the total transition count, including all input access, random-bit requests, arithmetic and output writing. Every random-bit sequence obeys the clock; thus only finitely many random bits affect each run. A malformed factor list, an incorrect list and the failure symbol all count as failure on a positive input. The algorithm receives no promise that N is semiprime or belongs to a particular distribution, no advice or precomputed factors, no order-finding or factoring oracle, and no quantum or unit-cost operations on unbounded integers. The task is full factorization, not merely deciding whether N is prime.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one algorithm and constants satisfy the all-input success guarantee and the all-random-sequences polynomial clock, or prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. A negative proof must exclude arbitrary uniform classical randomized algorithms with arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents; excluding deterministic algorithms alone does not suffice. For the affirmative answer, correctness includes every prime base, multiplicity, ordering and product in the complete output. A heuristic complexity estimate, a guarantee for sampled or restricted inputs, or a quantum algorithm does not meet the stated classical worst-case target.
cards.why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.

importance.reason: A defining open problem of computational number theory, with broad consequences for cryptography, arithmetic algorithms, and classical-versus-quantum computation.

progress.text: Shor establishes polynomial-time quantum factorization. The full paper’s January 1996 revision explicitly uses quantum computation, which is outside the classical randomized machine model of this card.
Agrawal, Kayal and Saxena publish deterministic polynomial-time primality testing. This makes prime-factor lists efficiently checkable but does not provide their discovery.

Harvey and Hittmeir prove complete deterministic factorization in \(O(N^{1/5}(\log N)^{16/5}/(\log\log N)^{3/5})\) bit operations as N tends to infinity. The 2022 journal result improves a logarithmic factor while retaining an exponential dependence on binary input length.

Harvey and Hittmeir’s revision removes the previous power-of-N lower restriction on the large-order threshold and slightly improves its runtime factor. Theorem 1.1 may return a large-order element instead of a divisor, and Section 1.1 still explicitly identifies polynomial-time factoring as unknown.

context_blocks.text: Multiplying the prime factors is easy, and the factors themselves fit in a polynomial-size output. Discovering them is the unresolved step. Trial division up to \(\sqrt{N}\) is polynomial in the number’s value but exponential in its binary input length. The distinction between N and log N is essential even when a newer algorithm improves the power of N substantially.

Primality testing and factorization are different tasks. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm decides in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime, without necessarily exhibiting a divisor when the answer is composite. It also makes a proposed full factorization efficiently checkable: verify that every listed base is prime and that the product is N.

Efficient verification makes the two common randomized formulations equivalent in existence: bounded-error polynomial worst-case time, and always-correct polynomial expected time with possible nontermination only on a probability-zero set of random tapes. This equivalence uses an all-input expected bound and fresh independent randomness, and the expected-time formulation alone does not give a worst-case clock on each run. The card chooses the bounded-clock formulation to state the success event without any runtime averaging.

The general number field sieve has the familiar heuristic expected-time estimate \(\exp (((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(\ln  N)^{1/3}(\ln  \ln  N)^{2/3})\). This is subexponential but still superpolynomial in the bit length. Rigorous deterministic bounds of \(N^{1/5+o(1)}\) make a different tradeoff and remain exponential in that length. Neither bound is a proof that faster classical factoring is impossible.
Shor’s quantum algorithm factors in polynomial time, using quantum order finding. It provides an upper bound in the quantum model and does not establish a classical lower bound.

The newer deterministic large-order theorem has a different output contract: it may produce a certified high-order group element instead of a divisor. Even when the requested order threshold is small and the subroutine is fast, that output alternative does not amount to a complete factorization. Its usefulness within factoring algorithms must not be mistaken for a solution of the entire factoring problem.

A classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm would undermine the corresponding cryptographic hardness assumptions. Neither the efficiency of multiplication nor a conjectured separation \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) provides a proved classical factoring lower bound. Factoring and inverting RSA are also distinct problems; the historical source explains that the reverse general reduction is unknown.
